# Introduction

## Global Burden of Obesity

Obesity has emerged as one of the defining chronic disease epidemics of the modern era, affecting populations across every income stratum and geographic region. The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration's landmark pooled analysis, drawing on 1,698 population-based measurement studies encompassing 19.2 million participants across 200 countries, documented a near-doubling of age-standardised obesity prevalence between 1975 and 2014 and projected that more than one billion adults would meet the World Health Organization definition of obesity by 2022 [@NCDRiskFactor2016Trends]. The mortality burden attributable to excess adiposity is staggering: the Global Burden of Disease 2015 study estimated that overweight and obesity together caused approximately 4 million deaths per year worldwide, with cardiovascular disease accounting for the majority of this mortality and metabolic, musculoskeletal, and neoplastic causes contributing substantially to the remainder [@GBD20152017Health]. In the United States specifically, national survey data indicate that adult obesity prevalence has reached approximately 42%, representing more than a doubling since the early 1980s [@Chooi2019Epidemiology]. The macroeconomic consequences are commensurate with this clinical burden: @Cawley2012Medical applied instrumental variables methodology to nationally representative data and estimated that obesity-attributable medical care expenditure in the United States alone amounts to approximately $190 billion per year, equivalent to 20.6% of total national health care spending at the time of that analysis. These figures confirm that obesity is not merely a clinical challenge but a systemic socioeconomic crisis demanding effective, scalable therapeutic responses.

## Definition, Classification, and the Limitations of BMI

Clinically, obesity is conventionally defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or above, with class I obesity spanning 30.0–34.9 kg/m², class II spanning 35.0–39.9 kg/m², and class III (sometimes termed severe or morbid obesity) defined by a BMI of 40 kg/m² or above [@Apovian2015Pharmacological; @Garvey2016American]. BMI thresholds are operationally convenient and epidemiologically reproducible, but the metric carries well-recognised conceptual limitations: it does not distinguish lean from adipose mass, fails to capture the anatomical distribution of fat — a critical determinant of cardiometabolic risk — and systematically misclassifies individuals who are metabolically unhealthy at normal weight (the "normal-weight obese" phenotype) or metabolically healthy despite elevated BMI [@Flegal2013Association; @Bluher2019Obesity]. These inadequacies have motivated the articulation of an adiposity-based chronic disease (ABCD) conceptual framework, formally endorsed by the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the American College of Endocrinology, which situates excess adiposity alongside its staging-relevant complications rather than reducing diagnosis to a single anthropometric cut-point [@Garvey2016American]. Central to this reconceptualisation is the Edmonton Obesity Staging System, proposed by @Sharma2009Proposed, which stratifies individuals from stage 0 (no obesity-related risk factors) through stage 4 (severe end-organ damage or disability), explicitly directing clinicians to treat the disease and its consequences rather than the number on the scale. This complication-centric paradigm has progressively influenced guideline development and trial design throughout the review period, with composite cardiometabolic endpoints supplanting weight change alone as the primary measure of treatment success.

## Pathophysiology: Obesity as a Chronic, Relapsing Disease

A foundational conceptual shift underpins all contemporary obesity medicine: the recognition that obesity is a chronic, relapsing neurobiological disease driven principally by neuroendocrine dysregulation, and not a moral failure or simple consequence of voluntary overeating. Central appetite regulation in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus integrates signals from adipose-derived leptin, pancreatic insulin, gastric ghrelin, and gut-derived peptide YY and GLP-1 via the gut-brain axis; chronic positive energy balance induces leptin resistance, blunting the anorectic signalling that would ordinarily constrain intake [@Drucker2018Mechanisms; @Muller2019Glucagon]. The hedonic dopaminergic reward circuitry overlays this homeostatic system, rendering calorically dense foods disproportionately reinforcing and creating persistent behavioural drives that resist consciously directed restraint [@Muller2022Antiobesity]. Genetic architecture contributes substantially to individual susceptibility: genome-wide association studies have identified more than 900 BMI-associated loci, collectively explaining approximately 6% of trait variance, though rare monogenic causes (e.g., MC4R, LEP, LEPR pathogenic variants) account for a clinically important subset of severe early-onset obesity [@Bluher2019Obesity]. The gut microbiome adds a further layer of complexity; seminal gnotobiotic mouse experiments demonstrated that colonisation with an obesity-associated microbiome confers a greater capacity for energy harvest from identical diets relative to a lean microbiome [@Turnbaugh2006Obesity], and dysbiosis-related alterations in short-chain fatty acid signalling and bile acid metabolism modulate both energy balance and insulin sensitivity in humans [@Fasshauer2015Adipokines]. Taken together, these intersecting neuroendocrine, genetic, and environmental mechanisms explain not only the difficulty of sustained weight loss through volitional means but also the biological tendency to regain weight following any intervention that is discontinued, a phenomenon strikingly illustrated by the STEP 1 trial extension, in which participants who discontinued semaglutide regained two-thirds of their prior weight loss within one year [@Wilding2022Weight].

## The Treatment Landscape and Why Each Modality Matters

Understanding the continuum of obesity treatment requires appreciating both the incremental contributions and the distinct limitations of each therapeutic modality. Lifestyle intervention — combining caloric restriction, increased physical activity, and behavioural counselling — remains the foundation of treatment and the entry point recommended by every major guideline. The Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), the most rigorously conducted lifestyle intervention trial, demonstrated that an intensive programme targeting a 7% weight loss through dietary change and 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week achieved a mean weight reduction of 5.6 kg sustained over 2.8 years and reduced the incidence of type 2 diabetes by 58% in high-risk adults [@Knowler2002Reduction]. The Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study produced comparable findings [@Tuomilehto2001Prevention]. However, the Look AHEAD trial — the largest and longest lifestyle intervention trial in persons with established type 2 diabetes, enrolling 5,145 participants and following them for a median of 9.6 years — found that, despite achieving greater weight loss and fitness improvement than the control arm, the intervention did not significantly reduce the rate of cardiovascular events [@LookAHEAD2013Cardiovascular]. This landmark null result underscored the limits of lifestyle intervention alone for hard clinical endpoints and strengthened the case for adjunctive pharmacological and surgical approaches in eligible patients.

Pharmacotherapy for obesity has been available since the mid-twentieth century, but the agents approved before the GLP-1 era offered modest efficacy with variable tolerability. Orlistat, a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor, reduced body weight by approximately 2.9 kg more than placebo in the XENDOS trial [@Torgerson2004Xenical]; the phentermine-topiramate combination achieved 9.8% weight loss with the full dose in the CONQUER trial [@Gadde2011Effects]; and naltrexone-bupropion produced approximately 6.4% weight loss in the COR-I programme [@Greenway2010Effect]. None of these agents approached the 10–15% threshold increasingly recognised as necessary to produce clinically meaningful and durable reductions in obesity-related comorbidities [@Yanovski2014Longterm; @Apovian2015Pharmacological]. The approval of liraglutide 3.0 mg in 2014 — which produced a mean 8.4% body weight reduction versus 2.5% with placebo in the SCALE Obesity trial (n = 3,731) [@PiSunyer2015Randomized] — represented an important advance, and the subsequent demonstration in LEADER that liraglutide 1.8 mg significantly reduced MACE in type 2 diabetes [@Marso2016Liraglutide] established the cardiovascular safety and benefit paradigm that would define the subsequent generation of trials.

Bariatric surgery has consistently demonstrated the greatest magnitude, durability, and metabolic depth of weight loss of any intervention studied to date. Meta-analytic evidence from @Buchwald2004Bariatric and longitudinal cohort data from the Swedish Obese Subjects study [@Sjoström2007Effects; @Sjoström2012Bariatric] confirmed 60–80% excess weight loss with gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy, accompanied by reductions in all-cause mortality and incident cardiovascular events over decades of follow-up. The STAMPEDE trial further established that bariatric surgery produces superior glycaemic outcomes compared with intensive medical therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes, with 57% of surgical participants achieving HbA1c below 6.0% at five years versus only 6% in the medical therapy arm [@Schauer2017Bariatric]. Yet surgery remains accessible to only a small fraction of eligible patients globally, given requirements for specialist centres, operative risk, perioperative nutritional support, and enduring lifestyle commitment [@Mechanick2020Clinical], highlighting the critical importance of effective non-surgical alternatives.

## Why This Review Is Needed: 2016–2024 as a Transformative Decade

The years 2016 through 2024 constitute what may reasonably be described as the most consequential period in the history of obesity pharmacotherapy. The subcutaneous formulation of semaglutide — a GLP-1 receptor agonist engineered with a C-18 fatty diacid chain for extended albumin binding and a plasma half-life of approximately one week — received FDA approval for chronic weight management at the 2.4 mg weekly dose in June 2021, following STEP programme results demonstrating 14.9% body weight reduction in the pivotal STEP 1 trial [@Wilding2021Once]. Tirzepatide, the first agent to achieve simultaneous agonism at both GIP and GLP-1 receptors, was approved for chronic weight management in November 2023 after SURMOUNT-1 data showed up to 20.9% weight loss with the 15 mg dose — a magnitude previously achievable only with bariatric surgery [@Jastreboff2022Tirzepatide]. The SELECT cardiovascular outcomes trial, reporting in 2023, demonstrated for the first time that a pharmacological agent reduces MACE in individuals with obesity without diabetes, repositioning semaglutide as a cardiovascular risk-reduction therapy rather than merely an anti-obesity drug [@Lincoff2023Semaglutide]. Concurrent with these developments, paediatric indications were established: liraglutide was approved for adolescents aged 12 and above following the SCALE Adolescents trial [@Kelly2020Randomized], and semaglutide was subsequently studied in the same population with similarly impressive results [@Weghuber2022Once]. Novel multi-hormone receptor agonists — including the GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist retatrutide, which produced up to 24.2% body weight reduction in a phase 2 trial [@Jastreboff2023Triple] — herald a further generation of agents that may approach the weight-loss magnitude of surgery entirely non-invasively. Against this background of rapid innovation, a synthesis of the current evidence is essential to support clinical decision-making, guideline development, and the identification of gaps warranting further investigation.

## Objectives

This systematic review aims to address the following pre-specified objectives:

1. To systematically evaluate the efficacy of currently approved anti-obesity pharmacotherapies — including GLP-1 receptor agonists, dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, and established agents — on body weight, cardiometabolic risk factors, and patient-reported outcomes in adults with overweight or obesity.
2. To assess the cardiovascular outcomes evidence for novel pharmacological agents in obesity, with particular reference to MACE reduction, heart failure hospitalisation, and mortality across populations with and without type 2 diabetes.
3. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of bariatric and metabolic surgical procedures — specifically Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy — on excess weight loss, type 2 diabetes remission, and long-term mortality, and to compare these outcomes against intensive pharmacotherapy.
4. To examine emerging evidence for obesity treatment in special populations, including adolescents, individuals with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and those with established cardiovascular disease, identifying subgroups likely to derive differential benefit from specific modalities.
5. To identify critical gaps in the current evidence base — including the absence of head-to-head pharmacotherapy trials, the limited data on long-term safety of newer agents beyond three years, and the underrepresentation of diverse racial and ethnic populations in pivotal trials — and to outline priorities for future research.
